title: Service mesh and sidecars
subtitle: A service mesh moves mTLS, retries, traffic control and metrics out of your code and into proxies. Learn what that buys you, what it costs, and when to say no.

c.v: On Friday 27 October 2017, at 14:10, Monzo deployed a change to a payments service. Current account payments started to fail. The team rolled the change back two minutes later. The errors did not stop

Monzo used linkerd to route and load balance the calls between its several hundred services. Linkerd learned where each service ran from Kubernetes. At 14:18, engineers found that linkerd was sending traffic to
that no longer existed. It had stopped getting updates

At 14:26 they restarted all of the several hundred linkerd proxies. The new proxies could not start until the Kubernetes API servers were restarted too. By 15:13 every proxy was back, but no service got any traffic. Now the whole platform was down, including the app
At 15:27 the logs showed the real blocker. Linkerd crashed with a NullPointerException while it read
data. A new service, deployed the day before and then scaled to zero copies, triggered a bug between the linkerd and Kubernetes versions. Deleting that empty service fixed it at 15:31
The first fault was a bug in Kubernetes and its etcd client after an etcd cluster upgrade a week or two earlier. Monzo called the restart of every proxy a poor decision that made the outage worse
. The proxy layer touched every call. So when it broke, everything broke.

A service that tells the proxies what to do: routes, endpoints, rules and certificates. In Istio this is istiod
as if the network were simple. The proxies do the hard parts. Because the proxy is a separate process, it works with any language, and you can upgrade it without changing app code
A mesh does not remove network work. It moves that work out of your code into proxies that your team must now run. You trade code in many services for one more critical system.

To roll this out, start in permissive mode. It accepts both plain text and mTLS while you add proxies. Then switch to strict mode, which accepts only mTLS
per service, with no app change. Check the defaults. In Istio, the HTTP timeout is off by default. Failed HTTP requests are retried twice before the error is returned
That default meets your own code. Say your HTTP client tries each call 3 times. Each of those tries can become 3 attempts in the proxy. So one call can hit a failing service 9 times. This is
. Linkerd warns that services under constant retries can be taken down by them, not given time to recover

Timeouts clash in the same way. Istio's docs give an example. The app has a 2 second timeout. The mesh has a 3 second timeout with one retry. The app gives up first, so the mesh settings have no effect
. Mesh and app settings work on their own, and can conflict
Retry only safe requests. Linkerd says retrying a request that changes state each time "can be disastrous"

The Istio project tested version 1.24 at 1,000 requests per second with 1 KB payloads. One sidecar used about 0.20 vCPU and 60 MB of memory
. Multiply that by your pods. For 400 pods, 60 MB each is 24 GB of memory just for proxies. Real numbers depend on your hardware and config
In sidecar mode, each call passes through two extra proxies: one next to the caller and one next to the callee
. Each hop adds a little time, and the
latency before and after, on your own hardware.
The mesh is now on the path of every call. Its upgrades, config pushes and bugs can break every service at once. That is what happened at Monzo
. Someone must own it, upgrade it and debug it at 3 AM.
An error may now come from a proxy, not from your app. Engineers must learn to read proxy logs and mesh config.

Istio's own team listed the problems with sidecars. You must restart the app pod to add or upgrade a sidecar. Each sidecar is sized for its pod's worst case, so a lot of CPU and memory sits idle. And sidecars can break apps with non-standard HTTP code

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: "Which problem does the mesh solve that we cannot solve in a library?"
If the answer is only retries, use a library.
Do not adopt a mesh when you have a few services, one language, no compliance need for mTLS, or nobody to own it.
Pick one layer for retries. If the mesh retries, turn them off in the app, or the other way round. Write that rule down.
Set a timeout in the mesh for every route. Make the app timeout a little longer than the mesh timeout × attempts.
Roll out mTLS in permissive mode first. Watch for plain-text traffic. Then go strict.
Treat a mesh upgrade like a database upgrade.

q.v: In a service mesh, which part sits on the path of every request?

options.v: The data plane, meaning the proxies.

why.v: The proxies carry all traffic between services. The control plane only configures them and gives them certificates.

q.v: Your code tries each call 3 times. The mesh keeps Istio's default retry policy. A downstream service is down. How many attempts can one call make?

why.v: Istio retries twice by default, so each of your 3 tries becomes up to 3 attempts. 3 × 3 = 9.

q.v: Your app has a 2 second timeout. The mesh has a 3 second timeout with one retry. What happens when the callee hangs?

options.v: The app gives up at 2 seconds, so the mesh retry never helps.
The mesh retry runs first, then the app gives up at 6 seconds.
The two timeouts add up to 5 seconds.

why.v: Istio's docs use this exact case. The settings work independently, and the shorter app timeout wins.

q.v: What is the main reason Istio built ambient mode?

options.v: Sidecars could not do mutual TLS.
Sidecars need a pod restart to install or upgrade, and must be sized for each pod's worst case.
Envoy is too slow for HTTP traffic.

why.v: The ambient announcement names invasiveness and wasted resources. Waypoints in ambient mode still use Envoy.

q.v: You have six services in one language, a shared HTTP client library, and a two-person platform team. A teammate wants a mesh for retries. What is the best first answer?

options.v: Adopt it now, because every service will need one later.
Put timeouts and retries in the shared library first, and revisit a mesh when you need mTLS or many languages.
Use both, so retries happen twice.

why.v: A mesh is one more system to run and upgrade. A shared library solves this need with far less to operate.
